title: Async KV flush race & soft-OOM diary
content:
Summary:

This doc captures on-call notes, timelines, hypotheses, and an initial runbook for the incident where a soft-OOM surge correlated with an async KV-cache flush race and a continuous-batching regression. Impact: transient host-level memory spikes, elevated p99 generation latency, and tenant throttles for ~18 minutes across 3 hosts in us-west1.

High-level incident narrative:
- 2025-11-03 10:14 UTC — Alerts: host memory usage crossing soft threshold (75%->92%) on host-gw-12, host-gw-19, host-gw-21. Autoscaler applied backpressure; several tenants observed 5–15s tails.
- 10:16 UTC — On-call paged. Initial SRE triage: no obvious leak in recent deploy (last deploy was a non-runtime config tweak at 03:00 UTC).
- 10:18 UTC — Observed a pattern of frequent async_kv_flush tasks in the runtime task queue tied to the eviction path; flush tasks had large scratch allocations and sometimes retried immediately after partial progress.
- 10:22 UTC — Memory spike correlated with simultaneous N async flushes and a burst of microbatch arrivals for long-context requests. Host kernel OOM not triggered, but allocator returned >80% of resident through fragmentation -> process RSS bridged soft-OOM threshold.
- 10:32 UTC — Manual mitigation: reduced batching window (microbatch_max_wait) and disabled async_kv_prefetch on affected hosts via dynconfig. Memory usage started to drop over next 6 minutes.

Metrics observed (selected):
- Host RSS: baseline 42GB -> peak 81GB at 10:21
- Process heap arenas: active arenas increased by 32 over baseline during spike
- async_kv_flush tasks per second: baseline 2 -> 14 during spike
- Continuous-batching in-flight microbatches: baseline 6 -> 24 concurrent
- P99 token latency: baseline 120ms -> 3.8s peak

Immediate hypotheses (ordered by likelihood):
1) Async flush concurrency misestimate: an async flush path was dispatching per-shard flush jobs without coordinating global concurrency, leading to many concurrent scratch allocations and temporary memory blowout when combined with large microbatches.
2) Allocator fragmentation: flush scratch buffers triggered new malloc arenas; combined with long-lived KV entries and batch allocations, the malloc arenas grew and VRAM/RSS could not reclaim quickly.
3) Backpressure inversion with continuous batching: continuous-batching kept accepting new sequences due to stale admission signal while async flush slowed eviction free paths, producing head-of-line memory accumulation.
4) Rare double-queueing of the same shard flush due to a race with the eviction coordinator that re-enqueued a job after a partial failure. This would temporarily double allocation for that shard.

Evidence and logs to support/refute hypotheses:
- We found logs showing flush jobs for shard-17 on host-gw-12 retried 3x within 20s with ‘partial-write’ traces and each retry allocating ~200MB scratch. (see GitHub PR link and runtime trace logs attached in linked_artifacts)
- Allocator stats show a marked increase in number of arenas and retained memory per arena (jemalloc retained ratio spiked). Heap prof snapshots at 10:25 show many short-lived buffers from flush code.
- Admission controller traces show continuous-batching admission loop had 180s-old watermark counters on host-gw-19 (stale metric propagation from host-local metrics bus).
- No evidence of persistent leak after mitigation; memory profile returned to baseline within ~10 minutes.

Short-term mitigations performed during incident:
- 10:32 UTC: Reduced microbatch_max_wait from 25ms -> 6ms on affected hosts (dynconfig). This reduced concurrency of in-flight microbatches.
- 10:33 UTC: Disabled async_kv_prefetch for low-priority tenants to reduce flush pressure.
- 10:35 UTC: Increased eviction aggressiveness threshold so that small entries were eligible for eviction earlier, freeing KV residency.
- 10:40 UTC: Issued host-level jemalloc aggressive purge (remote-run) on host-gw-12 to reduce retained RSS while long-term patches were prepared.

Customer/user visible effects:
- Several tenants experienced elevated p95/p99 latency for ~18 minutes; one PLG customer reported a small request backlog and rate-limited error responses. No data loss.

Post-incident root cause analysis (working):
- Root cause is a combination of (A) unbounded parallelism in async flush path when multiple shards flush simultaneously, (B) allocator fragmentation due to numerous short-lived scratch allocations, and (C) stale admission metrics that prevented continuous-batching from throttling earlier. The flush retry case amplified peak memory temporarily.

Proposed corrective actions (short-term):
- Introduce a global async_kv_flush semaphore per host (limit default to 4 concurrent flush tasks). Owner: Marcus Li. ETA: 2 days.
- Switch flush scratch allocation to an arena-backed buffer pool (reuse) to avoid malloc churn. Owner: Rina Gomez. ETA: 5 days.
- Emit flush job telemetry (start/end/duration/alloc_bytes/retries) to tracing and add an alert for >4 concurrent flushes. Owner: Aisha Patel. ETA: 3 days.
- Fix admission metric staleness by adding heartbeat propagation and fallback admission using local short-window counters. Owner: Omar Haddad. ETA: 4 days.

Proposed corrective actions (longer-term):
- Rework eviction/flush coordination: make eviction mark-and-schedule flush idempotent so duplicate enqueue is rejected. Add CAS-style tagging for in-flight shard flush. Owner: runtime team. ETA: 4 weeks.
- Add end-to-end stress tests that exercise interleaving of large-context microbatches and concurrent shard flushes to reproduce the race in CI. Owner: infra+serving runtime. ETA: 6 weeks.
- Investigate switching jemalloc config in production hosts to reduce retained memory (tuning or alternate allocator) and measure impact. Owner: SRE + platform-engineering. ETA: 3 weeks.

Runbook drafts (for on-call):
- Pager triggers: host soft-OOM >80% for >2 minutes OR >5 concurrent async_kv_flush tasks on a host.
- Triage steps:
  1) Check host RSS and jemalloc retained (jemalloc.stats endpoint).
  2) Check number and status of async_kv_flush tasks (runtime /admin/flushs endpoint).
  3) Identify top 3 shards causing most flush allocations (trace ids in /admin/flush-trace).
  4) If concurrent flushes >4: enact dynconfig to cap concurrency to 2 for affected host-group and notify runtime team.
  5) Reduce microbatch_max_wait to 6ms on affected host-group to reduce admission windows.
  6) If RSS >90% and tail latency climbing: enable host-level eviction-aggressive flag and schedule immediate jemalloc purge.
  7) If unable to recover in 8 minutes: redirect new requests from the host via routing policy and spin replacement host.

Post-incident follow-ups (owners and tickets):
- Create runtime PR to add semaphore: PR #1379 (linked). Owner: Marcus Li.
- Create infra ticket to add stress test: INFRA-987 (owner: infra lead).
- Observability: add flush concurrency alert: OBS-652. Owner: Aisha Patel.

Open questions / unknowns:
- What triggered the cluster-wide burst of flush retries? (network flaps? transient IO backpressure?) Need storage team traces for shard-store responses.
- Are there tenant workload patterns that predict large flush bursts (large numbers of small keys churn)? Data team to prepare query by 2025-11-09.

Notes to self / on-call tips:
- jemalloc purge can buy ~3–6 minutes of breathing room but is noisy in metrics; only run with a short blip and notify on-call channel.
- When lowering batching window, watch CPU increase—tradeoffs matter for noisy neighbors.
- If you see repeated partial-write retries in flush logs, correlate with p99 shard-store latency (external storage).

Appendix: useful commands and endpoints
- /admin/host-metrics?host=HOSTNAME -> host RSS, arenas
- /admin/flushs -> list in-flight flush jobs (fields: shard, start_ts, alloc_bytes, retries)
- dynconfig set: runtime.async_kv_flush.concurrency=2
- jemalloc purge: curl -XPOST http://HOST/admin/jemalloc/purge

Draft is intentionally pragmatic and chatty — this lives in Drive as the working SRE canonical notes while followups land in tickets.

Next steps before marking final:
- Confirm PR #1379 passes canary on non-production host-group and run stress test.
- Get storage team shard-store latency logs for 10:15–10:30 to understand root cause of retry burst.
- Convert runbook steps into short Confluence runbook and add to on-call rotation checklist.
